title: Agoyin Sauce
author: Jemimah Ogunleye
desc: Three hundred millilitres of palm oil bleached ten to twelve minutes, onions fried until they begin to burn, then at least forty minutes on low until the sauce is very dark but definitely not burnt.
longDesc: This is the sauce people actually want when they ask for ewa agoyin, and it takes three things: the right peppers, a great deal of palm oil, and the nerve to bleach it. Dried bell peppers are soaked two to six hours until plump, blended coarse with pepper seeds and ginger, and then fried in bleached oil for a minimum of forty minutes on low heat. The endpoint is a colour, and it is a fine line — very dark but definitely not burnt. Burning the onions slightly on purpose, before the pepper goes in, is part of how it gets there.
ingredients: 2 tbsp dried whole crayfish, or 1/2 cup smoked fish (optional)
steps: Soak the dried peppers until plump — between 2 and 6 hours, depending on just how dry they are.
Add the pepper seeds, half a cup of water, the minced ginger, crayfish and bouillon cube, and blend coarsely. Blend smoother if you prefer.
In a well-ventilated kitchen, heat the palm oil on medium and bleach it 10 to 12 minutes, until it reaches the colour you want. Do not leave the pot unattended.
Lower the heat and add the chopped onions. Fry the onions till they begin to burn a little.
Add the blended pepper mixture, the ground pepper, the smoked fish if using, and salt.
Still on low heat, let it fry for at least 40 minutes, stirring occasionally so it does not burn.
It is ready when the sauce looks very dark but definitely not burnt.
chefTips: Ventilate properly and stay with the pot. Bleaching 300 ml of palm oil produces a great deal of smoke, the breakdown products in it are irritants, and overheated oil can catch fire.
The three things that make this dish, in the author's own words: the right peppers, enough palm oil — which is loads of palm oil — and bleaching the oil as appropriate.
Two to six hours on the dried peppers, judged by how dry they were. Plump is the condition, not the clock.
Burning the onions a little is deliberate. It is where a good part of the darkness comes from.
Forty minutes minimum, on low, stirring occasionally. This is a long, slow fry and there is no shortcut.
Very dark but definitely not burnt. The distinction is real and you will smell the difference before you see it.
Another named source explicitly does NOT bleach — 'heat the palm oil but not to smoking point' — and fries only till very dry. That version is NGA032, and it is a genuinely different sauce.
commonMistakes: Bleaching without ventilation, or walking away from the pot.
Using less oil, which stops it frying and starts it stewing.
Taking it past dark into burnt.
Soaking the dried peppers for only a few minutes.
sources: Adapted from the sauce half of 'Ewa Agoyin And Agoyin Sauce Recipe (VIDEO)', byline Sisi Jemimah. Quantities as printed: 300ml Palm Oil, 8-10 Pieces Dried Bell Peppers (Tatsahe gbigbe), 1 Medium Size Red Onion, 2-3 Pieces Cameroon Pepper, 3 Heaped Tablespoons Dried Pepper Seeds, 1 Tablespoon Ground Pepper (Atagungun), 1/2 Teaspoon Minced Ginger, 2 Tablespoons Dried whole crayfish or 1/2 cup smoked fish (optional), 1 Maggi Crayfish (optional), salt to taste.

Times and cues verbatim: soak the dried peppers 'between 2-6 hours, depending on just how dry they are'; 'bleach for 10-12 minutes'; 'fry the onions till it begins to burn a little'; 'Still on low heat, let it fry for at least 40 minutes, stir occasionally so it doesn't burn'; and the endpoint, the sauce should look 'very dark but definitely not burnt'.
Her three critical elements, verbatim: 'using the right peppers, using enough palm oil which is loads of Palm Oil and bleaching your Palm oil as appropriate.'

HEADLINE DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled, and one of the sharpest in the whole collection. This sauce bleaches the oil 10 to 12 minutes and fries at least 40 minutes to 'very dark'. 1Q Food Platter explicitly does NOT bleach — 'Heat the palm oil but not to smoking point' — and fries only 'till very dry but not burnt', with no time given (NGA032). The oil quantities differ by an order of magnitude: 300 ml here against 2 cooking spoons there. Both are published.

A third named version, Lola Osinkolu's, preheats the palm oil 'until very hot', fries sliced onion 10 to 15 minutes until browned, then the blended peppers 10 minutes, and gives the doneness cue as the pepper having 'changed from bright red to dark red' (NGA033).
FLAGGED, unexplained within one author's work: she bleaches here but does not bleach for her ata dindin (NGA026), a closely related fried pepper sauce on the same site.

SAFETY: no source consulted gives a bleaching temperature in degrees. The hazards named by various sources are heavy smoke, flash-fire risk if the pot is unattended or overheated, and splash risk if ingredients meet hot oil.
storage: 3 weeks refrigerated under its own oil, 6 months frozen.
reheating: Low heat. It is already deeply fried and improves on standing.
healthBenefits: Capsaicin is associated with raised thermogenesis.
Dried peppers are concentrated in vitamin A precursors.
Keeps for weeks, so a single batch of cooking feeds many meals.
culturalNote: The agoyin sauce is the reason the dish has a following. It is almost black, aggressively hot, and swimming in oil, and a seller's reputation rests entirely on it. The bleaching is what takes the sauce from red to near-black, and it is also the step that divides careful cooks — one names it as essential, another refuses it outright, and both have good standing.
